title: My game has progression, but I realized it doesn't have meaningful choices
author: AsnIsCrazyToo
selftext:
I'm working on an indie game where players build their own aircraft by collecting and attaching different modules, weapons, and upgrades.

Yesterday, I continued working on the first level, which lasts about 8 minutes. The difficulty gradually increases over time.

After playing through it myself, I realized something was missing.

The gameplay loop was basically: fight enemies, collect parts, attach more weapons, become stronger, and repeat.

It was satisfying to watch my aircraft grow bigger and more powerful, but after a while, it started to feel a bit mindless.

I think the biggest problem is the lack of meaningful choices.

Right now, getting another weapon is almost always a good thing. There's very little reason to think about what to attach, where to attach it, or what to sacrifice.

I'm starting to realize that progression and meaningful decision-making are two different things.

I don't want to lose the fun of constantly building a bigger and crazier aircraft. That's actually one of the things I enjoy most about the game.

But I also want players to make interesting decisions instead of simply stacking more weapons.

So I've decided to keep polishing these 8 minutes before expanding the game further.

I'm curious how other developers approach this.

**How do you create meaningful choices in a game built around collecting upgrades, without taking away the fun of becoming increasingly powerful?**

comments.author: 0bscuris
comments.body:
Yeah, looks like you already got it. In order for a choice to be interesting there needs to be a trade off. 

Traditionally they handle this with a couple methods: 

using a triangle so for example blue is good against red but weak against green, red is good against green but bad against blue, green is good against blue but weak against red. 

I’m using colors cuz it can be anything so like, fast guns against light enemies, doesn’t get through tough enemy shields is basically same thing. 

Another limiter is ammunition, or mana or any other resource. Why when you play a first person shooter can u find tons of pistol ammo but only a few rpg rounds? So u can’t spam the rpg. 

Might want to take a look at mech warrior, they really have nailed these trade offs pretty well.

replies.author: AsnIsCrazyToo
replies.body: Thanks a lot for the thoughtful advice! The trade-off concept really makes sense, and your examples helped me see the problem more clearly. I'll definitely check out MechWarrior for inspiration. Really appreciate you taking the time to explain this!

comments.author: Harlan_42
comments.body:
We have our past experience of game playing to fall back on.  I remember a mortar game that started with just mortars, boring.  But as you progressed in the game, they add new and better weapons to tank.  We literally had nuclear weapons to take out a lot of real estate.

Thinking about your game, I would run progressive missions where they choose which toys they bolt on to get them done.  Maybe allow the player to build schematics they can use to prototype, like bomber mission's vs dog fights. Or for long mission's extra fuel tanks, for short missions more bombs for destruction.  Also made add rank as they move up.  

Game need purpose, but they also need rewards for the instant gratification.  Look for other story lines you can roll in that work with the purpose but add achievement by rewards.
